claims.text: The target material is a compositionally homogeneous, single-phase, equiatomic quaternary FCC solid-solution alloy.
The initial alloy has a high dislocation density.
Below 100 K, the alloy's yield strength becomes insensitive to strain rate.
Cryogenic strain-rate insensitivity is caused by saturation of dislocation-glide mechanisms.
Friction stress caused by differences in constituent-atom lattice parameters impedes dislocation motion.
Lattice-parameter-induced friction specifically hinders partial dislocation motion.
Chemical short-range order contributes to the high friction stress opposing dislocation motion.
At cryogenic temperature, thermal energy is insufficient for dislocations to overcome the friction stress.
Plastic deformation at cryogenic temperature is governed by athermal dislocation glide.
Athermal dislocation glide makes yield strength insensitive to strain rate.
Increasing temperature thermally assists dislocation motion and restores strain-rate sensitivity.
Diffusion-controlled dislocation creep dominates deformation at sufficiently high temperature.
Yield-strength-versus-strain-rate curves exhibit a plateau below 100 K.
Above 300 K, yield strength has a strong positive dependence on strain rate.
The transition from a rate-insensitive plateau to rate-sensitive yielding coincides with the onset of significant thermally activated dislocation glide.
Standard FCC alloys retain a positive strain-rate dependence of yield strength across all temperatures because yielding is thermally activated.
The proposed rate-insensitive regime is limited to single-phase equiatomic FCC alloys having substantial lattice-parameter mismatch and high friction stress.
The hypothesis fails when deformation-induced FCC-to-HCP transformation or deformation twinning dominates plasticity.
Differences in stacking-fault energy in the unspecified quaternary alloy could change the balance among glide, twinning, and phase transformation.
Nano-precipitates or grain-boundary segregation could introduce competing strengthening mechanisms that obscure strain-rate insensitivity.

contradictions.description: The stated 10^-4 to 10^-1 s^-1 interval spans three decades, not four orders of magnitude as claimed in the conditions, while the falsification experiment varies strain rate by only a factor of 100, or two decades.
